solutions.check: 29 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Frank's finished with revolutionary group

blocks.note: time's up means time is finished
a front is a political movement, as in a popular or liberation front

explanation.surface: Someone called Frank has quit a radical political organisation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frank' looks like a man's name, but it is the adjective meaning candid; the 's is just 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone upfront is open and honest about their intentions, a close synonym of candid or direct.

clue.text: All urinate everywhere? Just on the one side

indicators.note: spread everywhere, the letters end up scattered and must be gathered into a new order

blocks.note: the ten letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A puzzled complaint about a messy toilet user who should aim at only one side.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye's crossword enjoys schoolboy smut; the crude picture hides a ten-letter anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Unilateral describes action taken by only one party or affecting only one side, rather than both.

clue.text: Impartial IRA? F-off!

indicators.note: food that has gone off is spoiled, so these letters are spoiled into a different order

blocks.note: taken as written
the single letter taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone rudely tells the IRA to go away while questioning its claim to impartiality.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen in 'F-off' makes it read as an expletive, but F is fodder and 'off' tells you to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A fair judge is even-handed, treating all sides equally, which is what impartial means.

clue.text: Boris opened with "want member – not a union backer"

indicators.note: what opens a word is its first letter, so only the start is kept
one thing with another means the two go side by side in sequence

blocks.note: the opening letter of the name
to want for something is to lack it
a limb is a member of the body

explanation.surface: Boris Johnson begins a speech demanding an MP who is anti-union.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' suggests an MP or union member, but in crosswords it is usually a limb.
explanation.definitionFit: A blackleg is a worker who carries on during a strike, so he undermines rather than supports the union.

clue.text: Group of improvisers to obstruct Commons sitting?

blocks.note: to jam a passage is to block it
a sitting of Parliament is a session

explanation.surface: A comic suggestion that an improv troupe should disrupt a sitting of the House of Commons.
explanation.walkthrough: The Commons is the elected chamber of the UK Parliament; its sittings are called sessions.
explanation.definitionFit: A jam session is an informal gathering of musicians who play unrehearsed, improvising together.

clue.text: see 22dn.
Peer almost recruited into duke's bloomers business

definitions.note: the clue names the trade; the answer is the person or shop running it

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
a recruit is taken into the ranks, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: dukes is old slang for fists, as in 'put up your dukes'
a lord is a peer of the realm, here losing its last letter

explanation.surface: A nobleman is taken on in a duke's underwear company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloomers' looks like knickers, but here they are things that bloom, flowers.
explanation.definitionFit: A florist sells flowers, things that bloom, so a florist's trade is a business in blooms.

clue.text: Crown's wretched clan trapped by hunger

indicators.note: something wretched is in a sorry state, so these letters are knocked out of shape
a thing trapped by another is held inside it

blocks.note: to pine is to yearn or hunger for
taken as written

explanation.surface: A royal house's unhappy family is held captive by famine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crown' suggests royalty, which the surface leans on, but it means the top of something.
explanation.definitionFit: The crown of a hill or building is its highest point, its peak or summit.

clue.text: (& 17ac.) Clarification gone haywire – new technology for Big Brother's use?

definitions.text: new technology for Big Brother's use?

indicators.note: a machine gone haywire behaves chaotically, so the letters come out in disorder

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written; it doubles as part of the signal phrase

explanation.surface: An explanation has spiralled out of control, prompting talk of new surveillance kit for an Orwellian state.
explanation.walkthrough: Big Brother is the all-seeing ruler of Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four; the question mark flags the definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Face-scanning cameras that identify people automatically are a modern surveillance tool of the kind Orwell's watching state would relish.

clue.text: Labour leader welcomed by Hull as one who soldiers on

definitions.note: PLOD is a verb; read the definition as describing what such a person does

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so only the first letter is kept
a guest welcomed by a host is taken inside

blocks.note: the pod of a pea or bean is its hull
the opening letter of the party name

explanation.surface: The Labour leader is greeted warmly in the city of Hull as a stalwart who keeps going.
explanation.walkthrough: Hull is a city in Yorkshire, but here it is the outer casing of a seed.
explanation.definitionFit: To plod is to keep going steadily and wearily, which is exactly how someone who soldiers on proceeds.

clue.text: Brenda's measured strip?

blocks.note: first meaning: Private Eye's nickname for Queen Elizabeth II, a monarch
second meaning: a straight marked edge used for drawing and measuring

explanation.surface: The Queen performs a carefully judged striptease.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye has long called the late Queen 'Brenda'; she is one kind of sovereign, and a marked stick is the other meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: A monarch reigns over a country, and a graduated stick for measuring length shares that same name.

clue.text: Head of country, more mature, suppressing cry, is quite prepared to take breathalyser test

definitions.text: quite prepared to take breathalyser test

indicators.note: the head of something is its top, so only the first letter is kept
to suppress is to hold down and keep in, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
older people are more mature
to sob is to cry

explanation.surface: A grown-up head of state, holding back tears, is willing to be breathalysed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head of country' sounds like a president, but it just means the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone stone-cold sober has had no alcohol at all, so would happily blow into a police breath tester.

clue.text: Old bastard's not affected

blocks.note: first meaning: an archaic term for a child born outside marriage
second meaning: unpretentious, without airs

explanation.surface: A nasty old man is unmoved by events.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old bastard' reads as an insult, but it means a dated word for an illegitimate child; 'affected' means pretentious, not moved.
explanation.definitionFit: Natural behaviour is genuine and unforced, the opposite of putting on airs or being pretentious.

clue.text: Maybe Cheltenham has misused a resource to keep Conservative

indicators.note: things misused are put to the wrong purpose, so these letters are set in a wrong order
to keep something is to hold it within, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: taken as written
C is the standard abbreviation for Conservative

explanation.surface: Cheltenham, a famously Tory town, is accused of misusing funds to stay Conservative.
explanation.walkthrough: Cheltenham is a Gloucestershire spa town best known for its racing festival, the setting's example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheltenham hosts the famous horse-racing festival each March, so it is one instance of a track where horses race.

clue.text: Get out of the underworld, girl!

blocks.note: Dis is the Roman god of the underworld and a name for it
a miss is a young girl

explanation.surface: Someone urges a young woman to escape from hell or a criminal gang.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get out of the underworld' reads as one phrase, but 'Get out' alone is the definition, as a command.
explanation.definitionFit: To tell someone to get out is to send them away, the imperative sense of dismissing them.

clue.text: Novel on vain, devious Boris type

indicators.note: devious means taking a crooked route, so these letters wander out of order

blocks.note: taken as written
Boris Johnson was a Conservative, a Tory

explanation.surface: A book about an arrogant, scheming politician like Boris Johnson.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like a book, but it is the adjective meaning new; Tory is the everyday name for a British Conservative.
explanation.definitionFit: Something innovatory introduces fresh methods or ideas, which makes it new and original.

clue.text: see 9ac.
Get used to taking 'FU' time, from now on

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: to inure is to accustom or harden someone to something
the letters taken as written
T is the standard abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Someone resolves to get used to swearing at people from now on.
explanation.walkthrough: The rude initials are just two letters of fodder; 'Get used to' supplies the outer word.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases mean henceforth, describing every occasion after the present moment.

clue.text: Lie with bounder

blocks.note: W is a standard abbreviation for with
something that bounds is a hopper, like a kangaroo

explanation.surface: Going to bed with a cad.
explanation.walkthrough: A bounder is old British slang for a cad, but here it means anything that bounds or leaps.
explanation.definitionFit: A whopper is an enormous, outrageous falsehood, a big lie told brazenly.

clue.text: Embrace Cyclops and finally mention "clued fantastically!"

indicators.note: finally points to what comes at the end, so only the last letter is kept
something fantastic is wildly imaginative, so these letters are freely rearranged

blocks.note: the setter refers to themself, so their name means I
the closing letter of the word
taken as written

explanation.surface: A solver is urged to hug the setter and praise his brilliant clues.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often use their own pseudonym to mean I or ME; here Cyclops gives I.
explanation.definitionFit: To embrace something can mean to take it in or contain it as part of a whole.

clue.text: Modest drink and hack gets hammered

blocks.note: a half is a half-pint of beer, a small order in a British pub
to hack is to cut roughly

explanation.surface: A journalist starts with a small drink and ends up very drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hack' looks like a journalist, the surface's drinker, but it means to chop.
explanation.definitionFit: Half-cut is British slang for drunk, and hammered is another informal word for heavily intoxicated.

clue.text: (& 25/26/6dn.) Use extreme violence to forcibly separate two members

blocks.note: surface reading: an idiom for attacking someone savagely
setter's reading: literally pulling one arm or leg away from another

explanation.walkthrough: 'Members' suggests MPs or club members; read literally, they are two limbs pulled apart.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to attack savagely, and taken literally describes ripping one body part away from another.

clue.text: Part of a 'no venison' type of cooker

indicators.note: a part is a piece of a larger whole, so the letters sit inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the run starts at the end of the first word and stops partway into the last

explanation.surface: A section of a sign announcing a vegetarian-style kitchen device.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part of' looks like a single phrase, but the word 'of' itself supplies the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A fan oven circulates hot air with a fan, one particular kind of domestic cooking appliance.

clue.text: Vote against UN's one-time Secretary General dumping hot environmental hazard

indicators.note: one thing set against another sits right beside it
to dump something is to throw it away, so a letter is removed

blocks.note: a poll is a vote
U Thant of Burma led the United Nations in the 1960s
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on a tap, and is thrown out

explanation.surface: A ballot opposing a former UN chief who dumped scalding toxic waste.
explanation.walkthrough: U Thant served as UN Secretary-General from 1961 to 1971; dropping his H leaves the end of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A pollutant is a substance that contaminates air, water or soil, a danger to the natural environment.

clue.text: see 22dn.
Having a corporation brought before Gore – that's killing

indicators.note: what is brought before something is placed in front of it

blocks.note: corporation is old British slang for a pot belly
Al Gore, the former US vice-president

explanation.surface: A company is hauled up before Al Gore and condemned as deadly to the planet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corporation' looks like a company, but it is old slang for a large paunch.
explanation.definitionFit: Killing as an adjective means deadly, causing death, which is what fatal describes.

clue.text: see 22dn.
She's about to take name 'Cyclops'? Get knotted!

definitions.note: the clue's phrase is intransitive; the answer is the verb for being tangled up

indicators.note: about means around, so these letters are turned round into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
N is the abbreviation for name
the setter refers to themself, so their name means ME

explanation.surface: A woman is about to adopt the setter's pen name, and he rudely tells her to get lost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get knotted!' is a British way of telling someone to go away, but here it means to become tangled.
explanation.definitionFit: To enmesh is to catch or entangle in a net, so something enmeshed has become knotted up.

clue.text: Maybe bullet-proof member meets Hislop

indicators.note: two things that meet come together end to end

blocks.note: a limb is a member of the body
Ian Hislop edits Private Eye, so to the magazine he is 'our ed'

explanation.surface: A tough MP has a meeting with Private Eye's editor.
explanation.walkthrough: Ian Hislop is the long-serving editor of Private Eye, where this puzzle appears, hence OUR ED.
explanation.definitionFit: Something armoured is protected with metal plating, and bullet-proof is one example of that protection.
